extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from a legal treatise on what may be patented (principles vs modes), how far a patentee may appropriate scientific truths or known properties, requirements for the specification and claims, and procedural/pleading rules for actions at law for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability — principle vs mode of carrying into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot take out a patent for a principle; you may take out a patent for a principle coupled with the mode of carrying the principle into effect, provided you have not only discovered the principle, but invented some mode of carrying it into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge opinions (e.g., Watt, Jupe, Clegg, Neilson) emphasize that a patent must embody the principle in a practical mode (a machine or specific method). Example: Watt discovered condensing steam in a separate vessel and described a mode — patentable as a machine; mere statement of a principle without a mode is not. If the inventor has invented a mode of carrying the principle into effect, courts may protect against other modes that a jury treats as piracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of an embodiment described in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: You must have an embodiment of the principle, in some practical mode, described in the specification of carrying the principle into actual effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must 'particularly describe and ascertain the nature of his invention, and in what manner the same is to be performed.' Mere announcement of an idea (e.g., 'apply hot air to furnaces') without describing a practical mode is insufficient to comply with the proviso and not a proper patent specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of appropriation of scientific truths and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Truths of exact science and laws of natural science are common property and cannot be patented independent of their application; the extent to which their application may be appropriated is limited to what a jury considers piracy of the prior application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No general rule can be laid down; each case is judged on its peculiar circumstances. Courts recognize that you cannot patent a bare law of nature, but may protect specific practical applications to the extent a jury deems appropriation (e.g., Neilson's discovery of advantage of hot air).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of claim — claiming every shape equals claiming a principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If you claim every shape (or every form of achieving a result), you claim a principle; you must claim some specific mode of doing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walton's case (claiming elasticity to card backs 'from whatever source derived') was said to amount to a claim for a principle. The courts will reject or construe overly general claims that effectively monopolize a principle rather than a particular mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must fully describe means sufficient for purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the principle be given to the world, and that the means be fully described, and that the means, as described, be sufficient for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the principle is kept back and only particular arrangements are given (whether through ignorance or design), the inventor may not comply with the law and will fail to secure the full extent of protection. Full and enabling disclosure is necessary both for public benefit and to secure the patentee's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement analysis — substantial independent invention vs colorable variation
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether a subsequently invented mode is a substantial and independent invention or only a colorable variation (i.e., infringement), the jury should consider multiple elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors for the jury include: character of the original invention; the merit to be attributed to its author; the means by which the principle is carried out; the object of its application and the end attained; the success and utility of the prior invention; and the comparative merits of the two inventions. The question is fact-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of principle vs mere application — valuation in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who discovers a new truth or law and also applies it is of higher merit than one who merely applies knowledge already in the common stock, though legal property acquired may not differ in extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In infringement disputes the court and jury give greater practical consideration and weight to the original discoverer who brings new knowledge into the common stock; this affects assessment of merit, damages, and whether a later device is a mere variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications/adaptations of known properties may be inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications or adaptations of known truths, laws, properties, and qualities of matter to human wants constitute inventions which may be the subject of letters-patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many inventions arise from applying known properties (e.g., using caoutchouc to give elasticity). The law examines the object, means, and end of the application to determine patentability and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior failed or abandoned inventions on novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior invention failed or was abandoned, a subsequent distinct method may be sustained as new; had the former succeeded and been in use, the later might be held an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to whether the later means were merely obvious variations that a mechanic would devise. Examples include Kneller (earlier method failed; later method sustained) and the Neilson comparison where differences in means produced superior results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proviso compliance — mere announcement of idea is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere announcement that 'air shall be heated before it enters the furnace' or similar does not, of itself, constitute the subject of letters-patent nor comply with the specification proviso; a mechanical illustration or mode must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must go beyond stating the advantage/idea and must describe in what manner the invention is to be performed; leaving form of apparatus entirely to local discretion without guidance risks invalidity or inadequate protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent vitiation solely for generality of claim — fact-specific adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent have not been held vitiated merely because of generality of the claim; questions of claim generality must be decided on the special facts of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts guard against monopolization of principles, they have not adopted a blanket rule invalidating broadly worded claims in every instance; context, disclosure, and circumstances determine outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action at law — who may be plaintiff (parties to sue)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action for infringement must be brought in the name(s) of the person(s) interested: patentee, assignees, or grantees of the exclusive right within a specified part of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute (Act of July 4, 1836) permits grantees for districts to sue in their own names (a change from prior practice). Corporations may be defendants; practical standing rules vary with assignments and the interest held.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee naming rules in suit
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee has assigned his whole interest the action must be brought in the name of the assignee; if the assignment is of an undivided part, the action should be brought in the joint names of the patentee and the assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an assignment was only agreed to be made (not executed and recorded), the suit should be in the patentee's name; the assignment may be recorded after suit is brought but before trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording of assignment — timing relative to suit
rubrics_metrics.description: If the assignment has not been made but agreed to be made, the action should be in the name of the patentee; the assignment may be recorded at any time after the suit is brought and before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule allows actions to proceed while formalities are completed; but until assignment is executed the legal party of interest remains the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration requirements — show title with convenient certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration in an infringement action should show title in the plaintiff with convenient certainty and set forth all matters of the essence; without these, plaintiff fails to show a legal right to judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleading must affirm performance of all acts on which title depends. The declaration should proceed through the essential facts (see following rubric items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration must aver original and first inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should begin by reciting that the plaintiff was 'the original and first inventor' of the subject-matter complained of; this averment is necessary notwithstanding the letters-patent which are prima facie evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affirmative factual allegation is necessary because at trial the plaintiff must prove he was the original and first inventor; letters-patent supply prima facie proof but do not obviate the pleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration must aver novelty, utility, and no prior public use or sale
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should aver that the subject-matter was 'new and useful', 'not known or used before the plaintiff's invention or discovery', and 'not at the time of his application for a patent in public use or on sale with his consent or allowance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These averments support the patent's validity and title; failure to plead them may jeopardize the action. Citizenship averments are generally included in practice though necessity is unsettled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration must aver procurement of letters-patent in due form
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary to aver that the plaintiff, being the original and first inventor, obtained letters-patent for his invention in due form of law, under the seal of the patent office, signed by the Secretary of State and countersigned by the Commissioner of Patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleading must show that the statutory formalities for grant were observed; the patent serves as prima facie evidence but the pleading still must include procurement averment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration should set forth substance of the grant
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of the grant should be set forth — that the letters-patent secured to the plaintiff for a term (e.g., fourteen years) the full and exclusive right of practising the invention — and the invention should be described briefly as set forth in the letters-patent, with profert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing the invention, using the words of the patent is common; the declaration must connect the grant to the claimed subject-matter and make profert of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations as parties
rubrics_metrics.description: An action for the infringement may be maintained against a corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited show corporate defendants are subject to infringement suits like natural persons; procedural and jurisdictional rules applicable to corporations should be observed.
